title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
prompt:
Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (like 1, 2, 3, 4). The numbers can appear in any order in the array, and duplicates count once.

Write longestConsecutive(nums).

  • longestConsecutive([100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]) → 4 (1, 2, 3, 4)
  • longestConsecutive([0, 3, 7, 2, 5, 8, 4, 6, 0, 1]) → 9 (0 through 8)
  • longestConsecutive([]) → 0

Constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 10^5, values may be negative. Sorting would be O(n log n); the challenge is to do it in O(n) with a Set.

tests.name: a long run hidden in shuffled order, with a duplicate
two runs, the second is longer

hints: Trigger: "is x + 1 in the array?" is a have I seen this? question. Put every number in a Set so that check is O(1).

Idea: only start counting from a number that begins a run, which you can test with !set.has(num - 1). From a start, count upward while the next number is in the set. Each number is then walked over at most once in total.

Code shape: const present = new Set(nums); for (const num of present) { if (present.has(num - 1)) continue; let len = 1; while (present.has(num + len)) len++; longest = Math.max(longest, len); }. Loop over the set, not the array, so duplicates don't restart the same run.
explain:
Time O(n), space O(n). There is a while inside the for, but it only runs from the start of each run, so every number is visited by the while at most once across the whole function: about 2n steps in total. That "count the total work, not the nesting" argument is worth saying out loud; interviewers listen for it.

Without the start check, a run of length n would be recounted from every member: O(n²) on [1, 2, ..., n].

How to say it: "Sorting gives O(n log n). For O(n), I put everything in a set, only begin counting at numbers whose predecessor is missing, and extend upward with O(1) lookups. Each number is touched a constant number of times, so it's O(n) time and O(n) space."
